newsitem.title: USA: Starr's departure leaves Clinton guessing.
newsitem.headline: Starr's departure leaves Clinton guessing.

text.p: Kenneth Starr's imminent departure as Whitewater independent counsel will remove an irksome thorn from President Bill Clinton's side, but Clinton's legal problems are far from over.

Starr, 50, confirmed on Monday he will become dean of Pepperdine University Law School in California on or about August 1. While he said nothing about resigning as independent counsel, officials of the law school said he would step down.
"It's going to be a gradual transition process. On or about August 1, he will be assuming the full-time duties of dean," said Jeff Bliss, a Pepperdine University spokesman.

Starr, a hard-charging lawyer with impeccable Republican credentials, clearly nettled Clinton with his complex probe of the financial, legal and ethical dealings of the Democratic president and his wife Hillary.
The probe grew out of questions about the involvement of the Clintons in the failed Whitewater real estate venture in Arkansas, where Clinton served as governor in the 1980s.

It has since branched into such issues as the firing of seven White House travel office workers shortly after Clinton became president in 1993 and the suicide of deputy White House counsel Vincent Foster later that year.
When asked in a PBS television "NewsHour" interview last year if he thought Starr was out to get him and the first lady, Clinton replied: "Isn't it obvious?"

Even though Starr said the Whitewater investigation would continue "full steam" despite his prospective move to academia, Monday's news led to speculation that he had decided not to prosecute the president or Mrs. Clinton, who have denied any wrongdoing.

"The fact that he's leaving says there probably will not be any high-level indictments. You don't jump ship when you're the top man if the big payoff after all these years of investigation is just around the corner," Georgetown University law professor Paul Rothstein told Reuters.

"The timing, the non-partisan nature of the job Starr is going to and the type of person he is -- rolling all this together I think it's unlikely that action against the president or Mrs. Clinton is in the offing," Rothstein said.

But one trial lawyer said Starr's departure could mean exactly the opposite. "Whoever prosecutes Bill or Hillary Clinton is not going to be a popular person. It could be that having done the spadework, Starr has decided to let someone else take some of the heat," said the lawyer, who asked not to be identified.
The White House declined to offer its interpretation.

Asked about Starr's decision to step aside, White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters on Air Force One as he flew to New York on a visit with the president: "No clue what it means and no comment."
McCurry said that to the best of his knowledge Clinton had been informed of Starr's decision on Monday afternoon, when an aide took him a copy of Pepperdine University's press release.
Whatever the meaning of Starr's departure, Clinton still has plenty to worry about from legal challenges.

The Supreme Court is expected to decide by June if a sexual harrassment lawsuit filed by Paula Jones, a former Arkanasas state employee, can proceed while Clinton is president. Jones claims Clinton made unwanted advances toward her when he was governor.
And a flurry of potentially damaging probes are under way in Congress into the freewheeling 1996 campaign fundraising tactics of Clinton and his Democratic party.

Rothstein said the campaign fundraising scandal was potentially more serious than Whitewater because it went to the very heart of the U.S. system of government while "a lot of what happened in Whitewater is particular to this president and past history in Arkansas."
